title: Common breach scenarios and professional consequences
subtitle: Diagnosing accounts breaches, and where they meet the Principles and Code of Conduct
objectives: Diagnose an overdrawn client ledger, a premature transfer of costs, and an unbanked mixed receipt against the specific SRA Accounts Rules provision each breaches
Apply SRA Accounts Rules 2019, rr 4-6 to new fact patterns to identify whether, and how, a breach has occurred
Explain how an Accounts Rules breach connects to the SRA Principles and Code of Conduct obligations already covered elsewhere in this course, without needing to re-derive them from scratch

leadingAuthorities.role: Governs receipt, banking and transfer of client money — breached by premature transfers and mishandled mixed receipts
Governs the purposes for which client money may be used
Prohibits using one client's money to fund a payment for another client — the rule an overdrawn ledger typically breaches
The overarching obligations (already covered in this course's Legal System and Legal Services module) that an Accounts Rules breach almost always also engages

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This is the last lesson in the module, and it's deliberately less about learning a new rule than about recognising the same handful of rules in disguise — spotted from the consequence backwards, the way an exam question usually presents them.

profileHooks.weakApplication: Every item in this lesson's test pool is scenario-first. Expect to diagnose the rule from the facts, not recall it from a list.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: If rr 4, 5 and 6 aren't automatic yet, this is a good moment to glance back at the earlier lessons on each before working through the scenarios here — this lesson assumes you can name the rule once you've spotted the problem.

overview.hook: Most Accounts Rules breaches in practice don't look like fraud. They look like a busy Friday afternoon: a payment made a day too early, a cheque banked into the wrong account because no one checked what it represented, a client ledger that dips into the red for an afternoon because two payments crossed in transit. This lesson works through exactly those scenarios — and then follows each one to where it actually lands: not just a red mark on a ledger, but a question about the firm's integrity and the public's trust in it.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. The SRA Accounts Rules 2019, the SRA Principles and the Code of Conduct are all currently in force and stable; no relevant reform is pending.

parts.heading: Closing the loop: why an accounts breach is never just an accounts breach
parts.voice: reflective — sets the tone for the module's final lesson
body: Fourteen lessons ago, this module started with the observation that the SRA Accounts Rules 2019 run to only thirteen rules, but that the exam turns on exact mechanics rather than broad principle. That's still true here — but this final lesson adds one more layer, because in practice, and in the SQE1 assessment, an Accounts Rules breach is rarely tested in isolation.

You've already met the SRA Principles and the Code of Conduct in this course's Legal System and Legal Services module — the overarching obligations of integrity, honesty and upholding public trust in the profession, and the detailed conduct duties that sit underneath them. This lesson doesn't re-teach any of that. What it does is show you the specific point where an Accounts Rules breach — a mechanical, ledger-level failure — becomes something the Principles and Code also have something to say about.

That connection is what SQE1 is really probing when it pairs an accounts scenario with a question about consequences: not 'was a rule technically broken', but 'what kind of problem is this once you see it in the round'.

components.definition: The way a single failure — here, an Accounts Rules breach — can simultaneously breach a specific mechanical rule and one or more of the SRA's overarching Principles, engaging different consequences at each level.

interaction.prompt: This lesson assumes you have already studied the SRA Principles and Code of Conduct. What is this lesson's role in relation to them?
options: To connect Accounts Rules breaches to Principles and Code obligations already covered, not to re-teach them
To introduce the Principles and Code for the first time
To replace the earlier treatment of the Principles with a new, accounts-specific version
To argue that the Principles do not apply to accounts breaches
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — this lesson closes the loop between two things you've studied separately, rather than opening a new topic.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The Principles and Code were covered in the Legal System and Legal Services module. This lesson's job is to show where an accounts breach meets them, not to teach them from scratch.

parts.heading: Scenario one: the overdrawn client ledger
parts.voice: case-narrative — walks through the facts before naming the rule
body: A firm holds £2,000 for Client A and £3,500 for Client B, in the same pooled client account. A payment of £2,600 is needed urgently for Client A's matter — the fee earner authorises it, the payment goes out, and Client A's individual ledger now shows a balance of minus £600.

No money has left the client account that wasn't already there — the pooled account still holds enough in total. But that's exactly the problem. The extra £600 that funded Client A's payment could only have come from money held for other clients, including Client B. Client A's ledger going into deficit means someone else's money was used without their knowledge or authority.

This is precisely what r 6 exists to prevent: a firm must not use money held for one client to fund a payment on behalf of another client. It doesn't matter that the shortfall was corrected an hour later when further funds arrived for Client A, and it doesn't matter that no client actually lost money in the end — the breach occurred the moment the ledger went overdrawn, because for that period, Client B's money was doing work it was never authorised to do.

components.definition: A client's individual ledger balance falling below zero — even briefly, and even if the pooled client account remains in credit overall — which necessarily means another client's money has funded the shortfall, breaching r 6.

interaction.prompt: A client's individual ledger goes to minus £600 for two hours before further funds arrive to cover it. The pooled client account itself never runs short of money. Has a breach occurred?
options: Yes — the overdraft, however brief, means another client's money funded the payment, breaching r 6
No — because the pooled client account never actually ran out of money
No, because the position was corrected within the same day
Yes, but only if a client complains about it
interaction.explanation: The breach is assessed at the individual client-ledger level, not the pooled account level. A brief, corrected overdraft is still a breach at the moment it occurred.

parts.heading: Scenario two: the premature transfer
parts.voice: direct — a familiar mechanic, seen this time from the consequence side
body: This scenario should feel familiar from earlier in the module: a firm transfers £1,440 of costs from client account to business account two days before the bill is actually sent, confident the figure is correct. Two lessons ago this was framed as a mechanical question — was the transfer authorised at the time it happened. Here, the same fact pattern is framed as a consequence question.

The breach is of r 4.3: a transfer of costs requires a bill or other written notification of costs to have already been sent. Confidence about the eventual figure, or the fact that the bill followed two days later, doesn't retrospectively authorise what was, at the moment it happened, an unauthorised withdrawal of client money into the firm's own account.

What makes this scenario worth revisiting at this stage of the module is the pattern it shares with the overdrawn ledger: in both cases, the firm's own money and a client's money have been allowed to mix, even briefly, without the authority the rules require. That pattern — money moving before its rule-based trigger — is the thread running through most of the breaches an SQE1 paper will ask you to spot.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often reason that because the eventual bill matched the transferred figure exactly, no harm was done and therefore no breach occurred.
components.whyItsWrong: The rules fix the timing of the trigger, not just the accuracy of the outcome. A transfer made before the bill is sent is unauthorised at the moment it happens, regardless of how the figures later turn out to reconcile.

interaction.prompt: A firm transfers £1,440 from client to business account, then sends a bill for exactly £1,440 two days later. Has a breach occurred?
options: No — the figures matched, so no client was ever out of pocket
Yes — the transfer preceded the bill, so it was unauthorised under r 4.3 at the time it was made
No, provided the transfer and the bill are both dated the same week
Yes, but only because the sum exceeded £1,000
interaction.trapExplanation: Matching figures feel like proof that everything was fine. But r 4.3 is about sequence, not accuracy — the transfer needed the bill to come first, and it didn't.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Focus on the order of events, not the accuracy of the final numbers. The transfer happened before its authorising trigger — that is the breach, whatever the bill later said.

parts.heading: Scenario three: the unbanked mixed receipt
parts.voice: structural — works through the correct handling before showing the failure
body: A firm receives a single cheque for £2,000 from a client, representing £1,200 already billed and outstanding, and £800 further money on account for future costs and disbursements. This is a mixed receipt: part of it is the firm's own money (the billed amount, now a debt owed to the firm) and part is client money (the £800 on account).

The correct handling under r 4 is to deal with the whole receipt without delay: either pay the entire £2,000 into the client account and then promptly transfer out the £1,200 office element, or — where the firm's systems allow it — split the receipt at the point of banking so that £1,200 goes to the business account and £800 to the client account. What the rules do not permit is banking the whole £2,000 into the business account and leaving it there, even temporarily, 'to sort out later'.

That third option is the breach in this scenario: a member of staff banks the full £2,000 cheque into the business account, intending to transfer the £800 client element across once they have time. Until that transfer happens, £800 of client money is sitting in the firm's own account, unprotected by the ring-fencing the client account exists to provide — a breach of r 4's requirement to deal with client money without delay, however administratively convenient the shortcut felt at the time.

components.label: Handling a mixed receipt correctly
points: Identify the split between the office element (already billed) and the client element (money on account or unbilled)
Either pay the whole receipt into client account and promptly transfer out the office element, or split it at banking if the firm's systems permit
Never bank the client element into the business account, even temporarily
'Without delay' governs this exactly as it governs any other receipt of client money under r 4

interaction.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order for handling a mixed receipt of £1,200 (billed costs) and £800 (money on account) properly.
items: Identify the split between the billed, office element and the unbilled, client element
Bank the receipt in a way that keeps the client element out of the business account
Where the whole sum was paid into client account first, promptly transfer out the £1,200 office element
Client ledger correctly shows £800 remaining as client money
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the correct handling — identify the split first, keep the client element out of the business account at every stage, and only then transfer the office element across.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order — the split has to be identified before any banking decision is made, and the client element must never sit in the business account, even briefly, while the transfer is sorted out.

parts.heading: From breach to consequence: the Principles and the Code
parts.voice: reflective — closes the lesson and the module
body: Each of the three scenarios above is a breach of a specific, identifiable Accounts Rule — r 6, r 4.3, and r 4 respectively. None of them, on the facts given, involves dishonesty; each is closer to carelessness or a rushed shortcut than to deliberate wrongdoing. That distinction matters, but it doesn't make the breaches trivial.

This is where the SRA Principles you covered earlier in this course come back in. Client money sitting, even briefly, outside the protection the client account exists to provide is precisely the kind of failure that engages the Principle of upholding public trust in the profession — because the entire reason client money is ring-fenced at all is to protect clients regardless of a firm's solvency, intentions or day-to-day carelessness. A pattern of such breaches, or a single serious one, can also engage the Code of Conduct's reporting obligations, requiring the firm or an individual to notify the SRA rather than simply correct the ledger and move on.

None of that changes the mechanical analysis you've built across this module — you still identify the rule, work the figures, and diagnose the specific failure exactly as the earlier lessons taught. What changes is the frame around it: a solicitors' accounts question is very often, underneath the arithmetic, a question about whether the profession's basic promise to protect client money has been kept.
That's where this module ends. The rules are few, the mechanics are precise, and the reason any of it matters was never really about bookkeeping at all.

components.definition: The Code of Conduct requirement, covered in this course's Legal System and Legal Services module, for firms and individuals to report serious breaches to the SRA — an obligation an Accounts Rules breach can trigger depending on its seriousness, separately from correcting the ledger itself.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that a non-dishonest, carelessly caused Accounts Rules breach can still engage the SRA Principles and potentially a reporting obligation?
interaction.explanation: The protection client money receives doesn't depend on why it was put at risk. Carelessness, not just dishonesty, can engage the Principles and, depending on seriousness, the Code's reporting obligations.

testPool.prompt: A client's individual ledger balance falls below zero because a payment was made before enough of that client's own money had arrived. Which rule is most directly breached?
options: Rule 6
Rule 8
Rule 10
Rule 12
testPool.explanation: Rule 6 prohibits using one client's money to fund a payment for another client — exactly what an overdrawn individual ledger necessarily involves.

testPool.prompt: A fee earner authorises a £2,600 payment for Client A, whose ledger shows only £2,000. The shortfall is corrected the same afternoon when further client funds arrive. Has a breach occurred?
options: No — because the position was corrected within hours
Yes — the ledger going overdrawn, even briefly, means another client's money funded the payment
No, provided the pooled client account itself never ran short
Yes, but only if Client B later complains
testPool.trapExplanation: A same-day correction feels like it cures the problem. It doesn't — the breach is assessed at the moment the individual ledger went overdrawn, not by how quickly it was later fixed.
testPool.explanation: The breach crystallises the instant the individual client ledger goes into deficit, regardless of how promptly it is corrected afterwards.

testPool.prompt: A firm transfers £900 in costs from client account to business account, then delivers a bill for £900 the following week. Which rule has been breached, and why?
options: Rule 4.3 — the transfer preceded the bill, so it lacked its authorising trigger at the time
Rule 6 — the transfer used another client's money
No rule — because the amount transferred exactly matched the later bill
Rule 5 — because £900 is too large a sum to transfer at once
testPool.explanation: r 4.3 requires the bill (or written notification of costs) to precede the transfer. Matching figures afterwards does not cure a transfer made too early.

testPool.prompt: A firm receives a single cheque covering both a billed amount and money on account. Under r 4, what must happen to the client-money element of that receipt?
options: It must be dealt with without delay and kept out of the business account, whether by banking the whole sum to client account first or splitting it on receipt
It may be banked into the business account provided it is transferred out within 30 days
It may remain in the business account indefinitely once the office element has been identified
It must be returned to the client and re-sent as two separate cheques
testPool.explanation: The 'without delay' requirement under r 4 applies to the client-money element of a mixed receipt exactly as it applies to any other client money.

testPool.prompt: A cashier banks a mixed receipt of £1,200 (billed costs) and £800 (money on account) entirely into the business account, intending to transfer £800 across to client account once time allows. What is the position while that £800 sits in the business account?
options: A breach of r 4 — client money is being held outside the client account without delay having been complied with
No breach, provided the transfer happens within the same calendar month
No breach, because the office element was correctly identified in advance
A breach of r 6 rather than r 4
testPool.explanation: Identifying the split correctly does not excuse banking client money into the wrong account even temporarily — that is itself the r 4 breach.

testPool.prompt: A firm carelessly, but not dishonestly, allows a mixed receipt to sit briefly in the business account. Which of the following best describes how this connects to the SRA Principles?
options: It cannot engage the Principles at all, because there was no dishonesty involved
It can still engage the Principle of upholding public trust in the profession, because client-money protection does not depend on the firm's intentions
It only becomes a Principles issue if a client actually loses money
It automatically amounts to a criminal offence
testPool.trapExplanation: It's tempting to assume the Principles are only engaged by dishonesty. They're not — the protective purpose behind ring-fencing client money means even careless breaches can raise Principles concerns.
testPool.explanation: The reasoning connecting an accounts breach to the Principles rests on the protective function of the rules, not on the presence or absence of dishonest intent.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following scenarios is the clearest example of a r 6 breach, as opposed to r 4?
options: A payment for Client A is made when Client A's own ledger holds insufficient funds, drawing on money held for Client B
A mixed receipt is banked entirely into the business account by mistake
Costs are transferred from client to business account before a bill is sent
A cheque from a client is not banked for three working days
testPool.explanation: Only the first scenario involves one client's money funding another client's payment — the specific harm r 6 is designed to prevent.

testPool.prompt: A firm's systems allow it to split a mixed receipt at the point of banking. It receives £2,000 (£1,200 billed, £800 on account) and correctly banks £1,200 to business account and £800 to client account on the same day. Has a breach occurred?
options: No — this is a compliant way of handling a mixed receipt under r 4
Yes — mixed receipts must always be banked in full to the client account first
Yes — splitting a receipt at banking is never permitted
No, but only because the sums are below £5,000
testPool.explanation: Splitting a mixed receipt correctly at the point of banking is one of the two compliant methods r 4 permits — this scenario shows the rule followed correctly, not breached.

testPool.prompt: What do the overdrawn-ledger, premature-transfer and unbanked-mixed-receipt scenarios in this lesson have in common?
options: Each involves money moving, or being held, without the specific authority or trigger the relevant rule requires
Each involves a client being knowingly deceived
Each can only occur in conveyancing matters
Each is a breach of the same single rule
testPool.explanation: The shared pattern is unauthorised timing or mixing of money — client and business money crossing a line before, or without, the rule-based authority to do so.

testPool.prompt: A trainee argues that because no client ultimately lost any money in the overdrawn-ledger, premature-transfer or mixed-receipt scenarios, none of them should count as a breach. Is this correct?
options: No — each rule is breached at the point the unauthorised event occurs, regardless of whether a client suffers an eventual loss
Yes — the rules only bite where a client is left permanently out of pocket
Yes, provided the firm corrects the position within a week
No, but only the overdrawn ledger counts as a breach without an eventual loss
testPool.trapExplanation: Outcome-focused reasoning is the trap running through this whole lesson. The rules are triggered by the event — the overdraft, the premature transfer, the mis-banked receipt — not by whether a client is left worse off at the end.
testPool.explanation: All three scenarios are breaches from the moment the unauthorised event happens; the absence of an eventual loss to the client does not undo that.

testPool.prompt: A serious, repeated pattern of premature transfers is discovered at a firm during a routine file review. Beyond correcting the ledger entries, what additional obligation may this trigger?
options: A Code of Conduct reporting obligation to notify the SRA, separate from correcting the accounts
No further obligation, since correcting the ledger resolves the matter entirely
An automatic criminal prosecution
A requirement to close the firm's client account permanently
testPool.explanation: Depending on seriousness, a pattern of breaches can engage the Code of Conduct's reporting obligations — a separate consequence from simply fixing the ledger.

testPool.prompt: Which of these is the correct pairing of scenario to rule breached?
options: Overdrawn client ledger → r 6; premature transfer → r 4.3; unbanked mixed receipt → r 4
Overdrawn client ledger → r 4; premature transfer → r 6; unbanked mixed receipt → r 5
All three scenarios breach r 5 exclusively
Overdrawn client ledger → r 4.3; premature transfer → r 6; unbanked mixed receipt → r 4
testPool.explanation: Each scenario maps to a distinct rule: r 6 for cross-funding between clients, r 4.3 for the billing trigger on transfers, and r 4 generally for handling receipts without delay.

testPool.prompt: A firm identifies a mixed receipt correctly but, due to a backlog, does not action the transfer of the office element for eleven working days. Is this likely to be treated as 'without delay' under r 4?
options: No — an eleven-day backlog is very unlikely to satisfy the without-delay requirement
Yes — as long as the split was correctly identified from the outset
Yes, provided the client is informed of the delay
No, but only because the sum involved exceeds £1,000
testPool.explanation: Correct identification of the split is necessary but not sufficient — the without-delay requirement governs the timing of the transfer itself, and a lengthy backlog is unlikely to satisfy it.

testPool.prompt: A firm's compliance officer says the three scenarios in this lesson are 'purely technical' and have no bearing on the firm's obligations under the SRA Principles. Is this a defensible view?
options: No — client-money protection failures, even without dishonesty, can engage the Principle of upholding public trust in the profession
Yes — the Principles only apply to conduct completely unrelated to accounts
Yes, provided the firm's compliance officer signs off on the ledger afterwards
No, but only where the client is a member of the public rather than a business
testPool.trapExplanation: Dismissing accounts breaches as 'purely technical' is the exact framing this lesson pushes back on — the mechanical breach and the Principles-level concern sit on top of the same facts, not in separate boxes.
testPool.explanation: Treating an accounts breach as disconnected from the Principles misses the point of client-money protection — it exists precisely to uphold the trust the Principles protect.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The recurring trap across this lesson's test items is judging a breach by its eventual outcome — whether a client actually lost money, or whether the figures matched up in the end. Every rule in this lesson is triggered by the event itself, not by how things turned out afterwards.
